Catastrophic Injury Claims in Washington: Brain and Spinal Cord Injuries, Future Care, and the Liens That Come Off the Top

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·8 min read·November 11, 2026

Your husband was a framer, and a pickup that ran a stop sign on the way to a job site in Spokane Valley left him with a spinal cord injury and no feeling below the chest. He is out of the ICU and in rehabilitation, Apple Health has been paying since his work coverage lapsed, and the other driver's insurer has already asked for a recorded statement. Everybody understands the injury is permanent. What nobody has said yet is that a case like this is mostly about the next forty years rather than the last six weeks, and that before any of it reaches your family, other people with statutory rights will be paid out of it first.

What makes an injury catastrophic?

Catastrophic injury is not a separate kind of claim. The phrase describes scale: an injury that permanently changes what a person can do, usually for the rest of their life, and that brings costs running far past the bills already incurred. Traumatic brain injury, spinal cord injury and paralysis, amputation, severe burns, and the loss of sight belong in that group.

The legal elements are the same as in any other injury case. What changes is nearly everything else: how much of the claim lies in the future, how much proof that future needs, how many other parties have a claim on the recovery, and how much depends on finding every source of insurance.

How long do I have to file a catastrophic injury claim in Washington?

In the ordinary case, three years. RCW 4.16.080(2) sets a three-year limit for an action for any other injury to the person or rights of another, and it governs most injury claims from a crash or a fall.

RCW 4.16.190 takes out of the limitation period the time a person was under eighteen when the claim accrued, or incompetent or disabled to such a degree that they cannot understand the nature of the proceedings, as determined under chapter 11.130 RCW. That can matter after a severe brain injury. It is a reason to look carefully at the facts, not a reason to wait, because whether it applies is something a defendant will contest.

If a city, a county, a school district, or the state is involved, a claim has to be presented before suit and a waiting period runs, which is covered in the article on claims against government entities. Claims against a hospital or doctor run under their own statutes. In a serious case, each possible defendant gets its own deadline calculation.

Proving the future: life care plans and economic loss

The largest part of a catastrophic injury claim is usually what has not happened yet. Attendant care, future surgeries, medication, durable equipment, home and vehicle modifications, therapy, and the care a family member is now providing for free. None of that has a receipt, so it has to be proved.

The usual tool is a life care plan, prepared by a professional who works from the medical records and from the treating physicians' opinions to list what care the person will need, how often, and at what cost, over their expected lifetime. A plan is only as strong as the medical opinions underneath it. Every line of it should trace back to a physician who will say the item is needed, because the defense will attack any line that does not.

Lost earning capacity is built the same way. A framer who cannot return to construction has lost wages, but he has also lost a working life, its raises, its benefits, and its retirement contributions. Vocational evaluation shows what work remains possible, and an economist converts the difference, and the cost of the care plan, into figures a jury can use.

Washington also lets a party ask for future damages to be paid over time. RCW 4.56.260(1) provides that in an action based on fault for personal injury in which an award for future economic damages of at least one hundred thousand dollars is made, the court or arbitrator shall, at the request of a party, enter a judgment providing for periodic payment of those damages in whole or in part.

Who pays for a case this size?

The honest answer is often that no single policy is large enough. A driver with minimum limits does not become better insured because the injury is severe. That is why a catastrophic case starts with a search for every possible source: the driver's policy, the vehicle owner's policy, an employer if the driver was working, any umbrella policy, the injured person's own underinsured motorist coverage, and any other party whose conduct contributed.

The personal injury overview on this site explains underinsured motorist coverage and how Washington divides fault among several parties. In a catastrophic case, both questions matter far more than usual, because they decide whether the recovery comes anywhere near the cost of the care plan.

The liens: who gets paid back first

Before money from a settlement or verdict reaches the injured person, others who paid for care may have a right to be reimbursed. Washington writes some of those rights into statute, and they are strong.

Apple Health and other medical assistance. Under RCW 41.05A.070(1) and (2), the Health Care Authority is subrogated to the recipient's rights against the person who caused the injury and that person's insurer, and may file a lien on the recovery to the extent of the assistance it paid. RCW 74.09.185 says that recovery on those rights shall not be reduced, prorated, or applied to only a portion of a judgment, award, or settlement, except as provided in RCW 41.05A.060 and 41.05A.070. RCW 41.05A.060 says no settlement discharges or compromises the lien without the director's express written consent. Two points cut the other way. RCW 41.05A.070(4) requires the authority's recovery to bear its proportionate share of attorneys' fees and costs, and RCW 41.05A.070(2) says the lien is not effective against recoveries subject to wrongful death when there are surviving dependents.

Workers' compensation. If the injury happened on the job and was caused by someone who did not work for the same employer, such as another driver, RCW 51.24.030(1) lets the injured worker sue that third person. RCW 51.24.060 then sets the order of distribution: costs and reasonable attorneys' fees are shared proportionately, the worker receives twenty-five percent of the balance, the Department of Labor and Industries or the self-insured employer is reimbursed for benefits paid, and the worker receives the rest. The recovery is subject to the department's lien, and RCW 51.24.060(3) leaves compromise of that lien to the department's sole discretion. Benefits paid in the future can also be offset against what the worker kept.

Private health insurance, employer health plans, and Medicare can carry their own reimbursement rights, which depend on the plan documents and on the state or federal law that governs each one. Identifying every one of them, getting the amounts verified, and negotiating them is part of the case, and a settlement that ignores them can leave the injured person personally responsible after the money is spent.

Structured settlements

A structured settlement pays part of a recovery over time, usually through an annuity, instead of all at once. For someone who will need care for decades, it can protect against the money running out early. It also locks in a payment schedule that cannot easily change if needs change, so the split between a lump sum and periodic payments deserves real attention, along with how any public benefits the injured person depends on would be affected.

Washington protects people who later try to sell those payments. The Structured Settlement Protection Act, chapter 19.205 RCW, provides in RCW 19.205.030 that a transfer of structured settlement payment rights is not effective unless a court or responsible administrative authority approves it in advance, on express findings that the transfer is in the payee's best interest, taking into account the welfare and support of the payee's dependents, and that the payee was advised in writing to seek independent professional advice. RCW 19.205.020 requires the buyer to give a disclosure statement at least three days before the agreement is signed, including the discounted present value of the payments, and RCW 19.205.060(1) says the chapter's protections cannot be waived.

Preserving the evidence

In a catastrophic case the defense will hire its own reconstruction engineers, physicians, and economists, and the evidence they examine has to still exist. Vehicles are repaired or salvaged within weeks. Event data recorders can be overwritten. Commercial trucks carry electronic logs and dispatch records. Business video is kept for days.

Written preservation demands go out early, to everyone who holds something relevant. The medical side needs the same care: complete records from the first ambulance run onward, imaging in its native format and not just the reports, and a running record from family members of what the person can and cannot do, because the change from before the injury is the case.

Where this goes wrong

The family accepts an early policy-limits offer from the driver's insurer without first finding out whether there is an employer, an umbrella policy, or underinsured motorist coverage, and the release forecloses the rest.

The case is valued on the bills so far, without a life care plan, and the future care, which is most of the loss, is never proved.

A settlement is paid out without resolving the Apple Health lien, which RCW 41.05A.060 says cannot be compromised without the director's written consent.

On a workplace injury, nobody pursues the third-party claim under RCW 51.24.030, or the department's lien and future offset under RCW 51.24.060 are not explained until after the money is spent.

The vehicle is salvaged, or the product is thrown away, before anyone inspects it.

Years later, a structured settlement is sold to a buyer at a steep discount, when the court approval process in chapter 19.205 RCW existed to test whether that was in the person's interest.

What a lawyer does here

A catastrophic case is mostly organization and proof. Locking down the vehicle, the scene, the product, and the records in the first weeks. Finding every policy and every responsible party. Assembling treating physicians, a life care planner, a vocational evaluator, and an economist whose work fits together. Identifying every lien early and resolving it as part of the settlement rather than after it. Thinking through structured payment and public benefits before anything is signed. And keeping the family's attention on recovery while the case is built around them.
